title: The quantum geometry of the chemical bond
authors: Gabrielle Carrel, Nishchhal Verma, Fatmagül Katmer, Leslie M. Schoop, Raquel Queiroz
abstract: Electronic properties of materials depend both on band energies and quantum geometry of electronic states. We relate bonding indices to the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), showing how chemical bonding dictates the momentum-space texture of bands, bridging chemical and physical descriptions of solids. We show the QGT decomposed into the three center bond index, weighted by their oriented area. Resolving these contributions by orbital pair reveals the donor--acceptor character that distinguish ionic, covalent, hypervalent, and metavalent bonding. We identify the bonding pattern for topology in materials: noncollinear three center bonds, which are the source of Berry curvature in solids. Bond fluctuation can be directly linked to electromagnetic response by resolving their energy spectrum, opening a quantitative route towards the design of physical properties of materials from bonding motifs.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework linking the quantum geometry of electronic states to chemical bonding motifs using the Quantum Geometric Tensor (QGT). It demonstrates that the QGT captures bonding character, distinguishing between ionic, covalent, and hypervalent bonds through specific fluctuation patterns. Crucially, it shows that topological features like the Chern number require the periodicity of a crystal, not just a finite molecule.
main_problem: The paper aims to formally relate chemical bonding descriptions (like bond orders) to the quantum geometry of electronic states, thereby bridging chemical and physical descriptions of solids.
main_result: The quantum geometric tensor (QGT) quantifies bonding, showing that topological invariants like the Chern number are only non-zero in periodic solids, and that extended bonding fundamentally changes the dominant electronic fluctuations compared to molecular systems.
method: The authors use $ab$ initio methods to compute the QGT, decomposing it into contributions from two-, three-, and four-center bond correlations, and relating these to measurable optical responses.
model_or_system: The study analyzes electronic states in molecules (e.g., benzene) and periodic solids (e.g., lattices), using the one-particle reduced density matrix ($ho_{\alpha eta}$) and the orbital-center approximation.
key_observables:
Quantum Geometric Tensor (QGT), Quantum Metric ($\mathbf{g}_{\mu
u}$), Berry Curvature ($\Omega_{\mu
u}$), Bond Indices (two- and three-center), Chern Number ($C$), and optical conductivity ($\sigma_{abs}$).
important_parameters: Bonding motifs (ionic, covalent, hypervalent, metavalent), excitation energy ($E$), and the spatial extent of fluctuations ($r_{90}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the orbital-center approximation and an independent-electron description, neglecting excitonic and local-field effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how the QGT is built from bonds, showing the quantum metric from two-center bonds and the Berry curvature from three-center bonds weighted by oriented area. Other figures compare fluctuation patterns and spectra across different materials.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first relating QGT to bond indices, then analyzing how bond fluctuations characterize different bonding types (ionic vs. covalent), and finally comparing the quantum geometry in finite molecules versus extended periodic lattices.
why_interesting: The deep connection drawn between local chemical bonding motifs and global topological properties (Chern number) provides a powerful, geometry-based framework for predicting electronic properties in materials, which is highly relevant for designing novel quantum materials.

The QGT is a sum over closed paths through three orbitals, α →β →γ →α. The product of the density-matrix elements along each path gives the three-center bond index bαβγ, weighted by products of bond-vector components. (B) The tensor’s real part, the quantum metric, reduces to a sum over two-center bond indices, bαβ = |ραβ|2.
